title: Jack and the Wobbly Square
synopsis: At Jack’s kitchen table, the friends compare a loose square stick frame with one stiffened by a diagonal brace; Jack corrects his guess while Gus invents a house for an invisible sheep.
continuity_state: Before: The farm shelter supplies have arrived from a flatbed and Dan’s blue box truck; the repair area is fenced off. Mr. Lee plans to replace the frame and roofing, and Jack has sketched the old roof in his existing blue notebook. After: Jack has recorded a tabletop demonstration of why a loosely jointed rectangular frame can rack and a diagonal brace can resist that motion. This is a simple analogy, not a full barn design. Mr. Lee and adult crew have prepared the replacement shelter frame; the telehandler has not yet arrived.

related_resources.reason: Supports limited technical facts, not the fictional outcome.

rationale_citations.story_anchor: The corners could move, so the square leaned sideways and turned into a slanty shape.
rationale_citations.editorial_rationale: Unbraced rectangular frames can deform by racking when their joints do not resist that movement.
rationale_citations.evidence_scope: The linked university, government, professional or manufacturer source supports only the described broad mechanism, not the invented character experience, building performance or listener effects.

rationale_citations.story_anchor: With a diagonal brace across it, the little frame was harder to push out of shape.
rationale_citations.editorial_rationale: Diagonal bracing is one way to resist racking in framed timber construction.
